result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_graph_name()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the name of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L7793-L7841){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_graph_name() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Graph name](/assets/graphs/get-graph-name.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph, tagged with the name it was created with, graph_name roads, shown as a tag in the accent color. The card returns that name, 'roads', and a note below it says a graph without a name returns None." width="100%"} Returns the human-readable name assigned to this graph through the `graph_name=` argument of `Graph()`. The name is purely descriptive: it has no effect on any algorithm, but it appears as "Name of Graph" in the `describe()` summary and is handy for telling graphs apart when you work with several at once, for example: - labelling plots, tables, or log messages when looping over a collection of graphs - keeping track of which dataset or experiment a graph came from ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph's name, or `None` if no `graph_name=` was given when the graph was created. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The name passed to the constructor is returned unchanged: ::: {#8ead65be .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(graph_name="Social Network") graph.get_graph_name() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 'Social Network' ``` ::: ::: Graphs created without a `graph_name=` simply return `None`: ::: {#10c2173c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().get_graph_name() ``` ::: Names make it easy to report on several graphs in one pass. Each graph here is identified by its name alongside its node count: ::: {#e582ff27 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graphs = [ ec.Graph(graph_name="ring").add_cycle_graph(n=5), ec.Graph(graph_name="hub").add_star_graph(n=4), ] {g.get_graph_name(): g.count_nodes() for g in graphs} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'ring': 5, 'hub': 4} ``` ::: :::
